notes: Jeremiah contains an unusually dense cluster of repeated names, all flagged explicitly below and on the relevant entries. Distinct individuals sharing a name: (1) 'Shallum' — King Jehoahaz's throne name (22:11) is a different man from Shallum, Jeremiah's own uncle and Hanameel's father (32:7). (2) 'Pashur' — Pashur the son of Immer, the priest who struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks (20:1-3), is a different man from Pashur the son of Malchiah, one of the four princes who had Jeremiah cast into the dungeon (38:1). (3) 'Malchiah' — Pashur son of Malchiah (38:1) is himself a different man from Malchiah the son of Hammelech, whose cistern/dungeon Jeremiah is cast into (38:6). (4) 'Zedekiah' — King Zedekiah is distinct from both Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, one of the princes present at the scroll reading (36:12), and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, a false prophet in Babylon condemned in Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (29:21-22). (5) 'Hananiah' — Hananiah the son of Azur, the false prophet of Gibeon who breaks Jeremiah's yoke (ch. 28), is distinct from the man named only as Zedekiah-the-prince's father Hananiah, a bare patronymic at 36:12. (6) 'Shemaiah' — Uriah's father Shemaiah of Kirjathjearim (26:20) is distinct from Shemaiah the Nehelamite, a false prophet writing from Babylon against Jeremiah (ch. 29). Also worth noting, though not a collision (same individual, not normalized away): King Jehoiachin is called by three names across the book — Jehoiachin (52:31), Coniah (22:24, 22:28), and Jeconiah (24:1, 27:20, 28:4, 29:2) — and 'Nebuchadrezzar' is KJV's consistent spelling throughout Jeremiah, unlike 'Nebuchadnezzar' used in Kings/Chronicles/Daniel.

babylonian_officials_at_the_siege.description: Named Babylonian officers present at the breach of Jerusalem, listed together with no individual narrative action beyond their titles.
members: with all the residue of the princes of the king of Babylon

temple_vessels_carried_to_babylon.description: Detailed inventory of the bronze, silver, and gold temple furnishings taken to Babylon at the fall of Jerusalem — no individual actor named, but a famous, heavily-detailed closing passage.
items: the pots, shovels, snuffers, bowls, spoons, and vessels of bronze used in temple service
basons, censers, bowls, and other silver and gold vessels

characters.name: Jeremiah
characters.perkNote: Grants a passive Ink/sec bonus representing steadfast prophetic output despite constant opposition — 'his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones' (20:9).

genealogy.father: Hilkiah, one of the priests that were in Anathoth (1:1) — a different Hilkiah from the high priest Hilkiah who found the Book of the Law under Josiah (2 Kings 22), the text does not link them.
genealogy.note: Commanded by the LORD not to take a wife or have sons or daughters, as a sign-act of the coming disaster (16:1-4).

funFacts: Called as a prophet 'to the nations' while still young — 'Ah, Lord GOD! behold, I cannot speak: for I am a child' (1:6) — in the thirteenth year of King Josiah (1:2).
God's opening word to him: 'Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee... I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations' (1:5).

Performed several personal sign-acts beyond the potter's house: wearing and burying a linen girdle until it rotted (13:1-11), and the inaugural vision of a seething pot facing away from the north (1:13-14).

Bought his cousin Hanameel's field at Anathoth with silver while Jerusalem lay under siege, a deliberate sign of future restoration — 'houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land' (32:6-15).
His famous lament on the human heart: 'The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?' (17:9).

verses.note: His call and commission, told he was ordained a prophet before birth.
His anguished complaint that God's word is like a burning fire shut up in his bones.
Buys the field at Anathoth from his cousin Hanameel as a sign of hope.
Cast into the miry dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech under Zedekiah.

characters.name: The Temple Sermon
characters.deliveredBy: The LORD, spoken by Jeremiah standing in the gate of the LORD's house
characters.purpose: Warns Judah that the temple building itself is no guarantee of safety — obedience, not the sanctuary's mere presence, is what God requires; delivered twice, once in chapter 7 and again, nearly costing Jeremiah his life, in chapter 26.
funFacts: Contains the famous triple rebuke: 'Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD, are these' (7:4).
Cites Shiloh, the earlier resting place of the ark, as proof God will abandon even his own sanctuary if the people persist in sin (7:12-14).

The second delivery (ch. 26) provoked priests and prophets to demand Jeremiah's death; he was spared only after the elders cited Micah's earlier, similarly unpunished prophecy (26:16-19), and Ahikam the son of Shaphan personally intervened (26:24).

verses.note: The original temple sermon, delivered at the gate of the LORD's house.
The sermon repeated; Jeremiah is put on trial for his life over it.

characters.name: The Potter's House
characters.deliveredBy: The LORD, through two enacted signs given to Jeremiah — the potter's wheel (ch. 18) and the broken earthen bottle (ch. 19)
characters.purpose: Illustrates God's sovereign right, like a potter over clay, to reshape or irrevocably break the nation according to its response to his word.
funFacts: At the wheel, the vessel 'was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel' (18:4) — judgment is shown as conditional, remade if the nation repents (18:7-8).

In the follow-up sign, Jeremiah buys a potter's earthen bottle and smashes it before the elders and priests in the Valley of the son of Hinnom, declaring the breaking irreversible — 'even so will I break this people and this city, as one breaketh a potter's vessel, that cannot be made whole again' (19:10-11).

verses.note: The potter reworking marred clay on the wheel.
The earthen bottle broken at the Valley of the son of Hinnom, a sign judgment cannot be undone.

characters.name: Pashur the son of Immer

genealogy.note: A priest and 'chief governor in the house of the LORD' (20:1); a different man from Pashur the son of Malchiah, one of the princes who later has Jeremiah cast into a dungeon (38:1) — see book notes.

characters.perkNote: Represents opposition survived — a bonus flavored around enduring persecution, since his flogging and stocks are the price of unwelcome prophecy.
funFacts: Struck Jeremiah and put him in the stocks at the high gate of Benjamin for a full day after hearing his prophecy (20:1-2).
Jeremiah renamed him 'Magor-missabib' ('terror on every side') and prophesied he and his household would die in Babylonian captivity (20:3-6).

verses.note: Pashur beats Jeremiah, puts him in the stocks, and receives a new, ominous name in return.

characters.name: Jehoiakim

genealogy.note: Elder half-brother and successor of Jehoahaz (called Shallum, 22:11), placed on the throne by Pharaoh Necho in Shallum's place; not to be confused with Jeremiah's own uncle Shallum (32:7), a different man of the same name — see book notes.

characters.perkNote: A hostile-court flavor — narratively offset by Baruch's persistence in re-writing what the king destroys.
funFacts: Personally cut Jeremiah's dictated scroll into pieces with a penknife and burned it in the brazier fire, column by column, after hearing only a portion read (36:21-23).
Contrasted unfavorably by Jeremiah with his father Josiah, who 'did judgment and justice... he judged the cause of the poor and needy... was not this to know me? saith the LORD' (22:15-16).
Jeremiah's fourth-year oracle under his reign first names the seventy-year Babylonian captivity (25:1, 25:11-12).
Ordered the execution of the prophet Uriah the son of Shemaiah for prophesying against the city and land (26:20-23).

verses.note: Burns Jeremiah's dictated scroll column by column.
Denounced for building his house 'by unrighteousness,' given a donkey's-burial prophecy.
The seventy-years-of-Babylon prophecy, dated to his fourth year.

characters.name: Baruch

genealogy.note: Brother of Seraiah the quartermaster (51:59), covered as his own submanager below.

characters.perkNote: The literal scribe of the book — grants a bonus to written/passive output, reflecting his taking Jeremiah's dictation not once but twice (36:4, 36:32).
funFacts: Wrote Jeremiah's words 'from the mouth of Jeremiah' onto a scroll at his dictation (36:4).
Read the scroll aloud publicly in the temple, since Jeremiah himself was 'shut up' and could not go (36:5-8).
After Jehoiakim burned the first scroll, wrote a second, expanded scroll at Jeremiah's dictation, containing 'all the words of the book which Jehoiakim... had burned in the fire' (36:32).
Received a personal, somewhat rebuking oracle from the LORD promising his own life would be spared 'for a prey' amid the coming judgment (45:1-5).

verses.note: Writes and then reads Jeremiah's scroll aloud in the temple.
Rewrites the scroll after the king destroys the first copy.
Personal oracle to Baruch, promising his life as 'a prey' in the coming disaster.

characters.name: Hananiah

genealogy.note: 'The prophet, which was of Gibeon' (28:1); a different man from Zedekiah-the-prince's father, also named Hananiah, mentioned only as a bare patronymic at 36:12 — see book notes.

characters.perkNote: A false-prophecy flavor — a bonus that looks strong short-term but is narratively unmasked, included as a cautionary counterpart to real production.
funFacts: Publicly broke the wooden yoke Jeremiah wore as a sign-act, prophesying Babylon's power would break within two years (28:10-11).

Jeremiah replied that Hananiah's broken wooden yoke would be replaced with a yoke of iron (28:13), and prophesied Hananiah himself would die within the year for making the people 'trust in a lie' (28:15-16).
Died two months later, 'the same year, in the seventh month' (28:17), exactly as Jeremiah had prophesied.

verses.note: Breaks Jeremiah's yoke and prophesies Babylon's swift fall.
Jeremiah's counter-prophecy and Hananiah's death within the year.

characters.name: The New Covenant
characters.deliveredBy: The LORD, spoken through Jeremiah, within the larger 'Book of Consolation' (chs. 30-33)
characters.purpose: Promises a future covenant unlike the Sinai covenant Israel broke — God's law written on the heart and sins remembered no more — the theological high point of the book's restoration oracles.
funFacts: Contains the explicit phrase 'new covenant': 'Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah' (31:31).
Promises the law written 'in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts' rather than on tablets of stone (31:33).
Closely followed by the messianic 'Branch' oracle — 'a righteous Branch... and this is his name whereby he shall be called, THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS' (33:15-16, echoing 23:5-6).

verses.note: The new covenant oracle, its law written on the heart and sins forgiven and forgotten.
The 'righteous Branch' restoration promise, thematically paired with the new covenant.

characters.name: The Letter to the Exiles
characters.deliveredBy: Jeremiah, by letter, sent to the elders, priests, prophets, and people already carried captive to Babylon
characters.purpose: Instructs the exiles to settle in for the long haul — build houses, plant gardens, seek the peace of the city — rather than trust the false prophets among them promising a swift return, grounding hope instead in a specific, dated promise of restoration.
funFacts: Contains one of the book's most quoted verses: 'For I know the thoughts that I think toward you, saith the LORD, thoughts of peace, and not of evil, to give you an expected end' (29:11).
Names the length of exile explicitly: 'After seventy years be accomplished at Babylon I will visit you' (29:10).

Names and condemns two false prophets active among the exiles in Babylon — Ahab the son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah — prophesying they would be roasted in fire by the king of Babylon; this Zedekiah is a different man from King Zedekiah of Judah, see book notes (29:21-23).
Carried to Babylon by Elasah the son of Shaphan and Gemariah the son of Hilkiah, who were traveling there on other royal business (29:3).

verses.note: Instructs the exiles to build houses, plant gardens, and seek Babylon's peace.
The seventy-year promise and 'thoughts of peace, and not of evil.'
Condemns the false prophets Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah.

characters.name: Jehoiachin (also called Coniah and Jeconiah)

genealogy.note: Called by three names across the book — Jehoiachin (52:31), Coniah (22:24, 22:28), and Jeconiah (24:1, 27:20, 28:4, 29:2) — the same man throughout, all genuine KJV usage, not normalized.

characters.perkNote: A removed-from-play flavor — a bonus locked away in exile, framed narratively around the signet-ring rejection oracle.
funFacts: The LORD declares that even 'though Coniah... were the signet upon my right hand, yet would I pluck thee thence' (22:24).
Pronounced childless for throne purposes: 'Write ye this man childless... for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David' (22:30).

The 'two baskets of figs' vision (ch. 24) is dated after Nebuchadnezzar carried Jeconiah into captivity — the good figs represent the exiles taken with him, marked for eventual restoration; the bad figs represent those left behind under Zedekiah, marked for further judgment (24:1-10).

After thirty-seven years of captivity, the book closes with his release and elevation at the Babylonian court under Evil-merodach, who 'did eat bread continually before him all the days of his life' (52:31-34).

verses.note: The signet-ring rejection oracle and the 'childless' throne pronouncement.
The two baskets of figs vision, dated to his captivity.
His eventual release and honor at the Babylonian court, closing the book.

characters.name: Zedekiah

genealogy.mother: Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah
genealogy.note: Judah's last king, installed by Nebuchadnezzar in Jehoiachin's place (37:1); distinct from two other men named Zedekiah in this book — Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, one of the princes at the scroll reading (36:12), and Zedekiah the son of Maaseiah, a false prophet condemned in Jeremiah's letter to the exiles (29:21-22) — see book notes.

characters.perkNote: A wavering-loyalty flavor — the bonus fluctuates to represent a king who repeatedly consults Jeremiah in secret yet never acts on the answer.
funFacts: Repeatedly sent messengers, including Zephaniah the priest, to ask Jeremiah to 'inquire of the LORD' for the city during the siege (21:1-2, 37:3).
Secretly summoned Jeremiah from prison to ask 'Is there any word from the LORD?' and received a blunt answer: 'thou shalt be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon' (37:17).
Allowed his princes to cast Jeremiah into the dungeon (38:5-6), yet secretly consulted him again soon after and swore an oath to protect his life (38:14-16).
Ultimately captured fleeing Jerusalem, watched his sons slain at Riblah, then was blinded and carried to Babylon in chains (39:5-7).

verses.note: Secretly asks the imprisoned Jeremiah whether there is any word from the LORD.
A second secret consultation, with an oath to protect Jeremiah's life.
His capture, the slaughter of his sons, and his blinding.

characters.name: Ebedmelech

genealogy.note: 'The Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs which was in the king's house' (38:7).

characters.perkNote: A rescue flavor — a padding/cushioning-themed bonus drawn directly from his use of worn-out rags to spare Jeremiah's armpits while pulling him up.
funFacts: Heard that Jeremiah had been left to sink in the mire of the dungeon and went straight to Zedekiah to plead for his life (38:7-9).
Given thirty men and the king's authorization to draw Jeremiah out (38:10).
Specifically took 'old cast clouts and old rotten rags' and let them down by cords to Jeremiah to put under his armholes before pulling him up — a small, deliberately kind detail (38:11-13).
Received his own personal promise of survival from Jeremiah: 'thy life shall be for a prey unto thee... because thou hast put thy trust in me' (39:15-18).

verses.note: Rescues Jeremiah from the miry dungeon using worn rags to cushion the ropes.
Receives a personal promise of deliverance for his act of trust and kindness.

characters.name: The Oracles Against the Nations
characters.deliveredBy: Jeremiah, 'the word of the LORD... against the Gentile nations'
characters.purpose: Extends Jeremiah's message beyond Judah — judgment oracles against Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, Elam, and finally Babylon itself — establishing that the LORD's sovereignty and moral accountability are not limited to his own covenant people.
funFacts: Opens with the vision of the cup of the wine of God's fury, made to pass 'unto all the nations' one by one (25:15-29).
The Babylon oracle (chs. 50-51) is the longest single oracle in the block, prophesying Babylon's own eventual fall even while it stands as God's chosen instrument of judgment against everyone else.
The scroll of judgment against Babylon was bound to a stone and sunk in the Euphrates by Seraiah, Baruch's brother, as a sign it would 'sink, and shall not rise' (51:59-64).

verses.note: The cup of fury passed to all the nations, opening the oracle block.
The oracle against Egypt, first in the sequence.
The long closing oracle against Babylon itself.

characters.name: Nebuchadrezzar

genealogy.note: King of Babylon; KJV spells his name 'Nebuchadrezzar' consistently throughout Jeremiah (with an 'r'), unlike the 'Nebuchadnezzar' spelling used in Kings/Chronicles/Daniel — a deliberate KJV spelling difference, not normalized here.

characters.perkNote: A conquest-scale flavor — narratively tied to his officials personally carrying out the siege and the temple's dismantling.
funFacts: Jeremiah repeatedly calls him 'my servant,' God's chosen instrument of judgment, though a pagan king (25:9, 27:6, 43:10).
As a sign-act performed at Tahpanhes in Egypt, Jeremiah hides great stones in the clay of the brick-kiln pavement and prophesies Nebuchadrezzar will set his throne over that very spot (43:8-13).
His officials, including Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, carried out the actual siege, breach, and burning of Jerusalem and the temple (39:1-10, 52:12-14).
The temple's remaining bronze, silver, and gold vessels — pillars, sea, bases, snuffers, bowls, spoons — are inventoried in detail as carried off to Babylon (52:17-23).

verses.note: Called God's 'servant,' given dominion over the nations.
Sign-act at Tahpanhes predicting his throne set over buried pavement stones.
The temple's destruction and detailed inventory of its vessels taken to Babylon.

characters.name: Gedaliah

genealogy.note: Grandson of Shaphan the scribe (40:5); his father Ahikam is the same man who protects Jeremiah at 26:24. A different man from Gedaliah the son of Pashur, one of the princes who casts Jeremiah into the dungeon (38:1) — see book notes.

characters.perkNote: A stability bonus representing brief, genuine order after the fall of Jerusalem — undercut narratively by his assassination.
funFacts: Appointed governor over the remnant left in the land by Nebuchadnezzar's captain Nebuzaradan (40:5-7).
Given Jeremiah's own choice of whether to go to Babylon under royal protection or stay in the land; Jeremiah chose to remain with Gedaliah (40:1-6).
Explicitly warned by Johanan the son of Kareah that Ishmael had been sent to kill him, and refused to believe it — 'thou speakest falsely of Ishmael' (40:13-16).
Assassinated by Ishmael the son of Nethaniah at Mizpah, along with the Jews and Chaldean soldiers who were with him, only months into his governorship (41:1-3).

verses.note: Appointed governor over the remnant of Judah.
Warned of the assassination plot and refuses to believe it.
Assassinated by Ishmael during a shared meal at Mizpah.

characters.name: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah

genealogy.note: 'Of the seed royal,' one of the king's princes (41:1).

characters.perkNote: A disruption flavor representing the sudden collapse of the post-siege order at Mizpah.
funFacts: Murdered Gedaliah and 'all the Jews that were with him at Mizpah, and the Chaldeans that were found there' during a shared meal (41:1-3).

The next day, murdered seventy of eighty pilgrims traveling to the temple with offerings, casting their bodies into a cistern — 'the same is it which Asa the king had made for fear of Baasha king of Israel' (41:4-9).
Took the remaining people of Mizpah, including the king's daughters, captive toward the Ammonites, before Johanan intercepted and freed them (41:10-16).

verses.note: Assassinates Gedaliah and those with him at Mizpah.
Massacres seventy pilgrims and casts their bodies into an old cistern.
Takes captives toward Ammon before Johanan intervenes.

characters.name: Johanan the son of Kareah

genealogy.note: One of 'the captains of the forces' who had remained scattered in the field after Jerusalem's fall (40:7-8).

characters.perkNote: A leadership flavor representing rallying survivors, offset narratively by defiance of prophecy at the arc's end.
funFacts: Warned Gedaliah of Ishmael's assassination plot and even offered to kill Ishmael secretly first; Gedaliah refused (40:13-16).
Pursued Ishmael after Gedaliah's murder and recovered the captives he had taken, though Ishmael himself escaped to the Ammonites (41:11-15).

Led the surviving remnant to ask Jeremiah for God's guidance on whether to flee to Egypt, swearing in advance to obey whatever the answer was (42:1-6) — then rejected Jeremiah's answer to stay in the land, and led the people down into Egypt anyway, taking Jeremiah and Baruch along by force (43:1-7).

verses.note: Asks Jeremiah for guidance and swears in advance to obey it.
Rejects the answer he swore to obey and leads the remnant to Egypt.

characters.name: The Rechabites' Obedience
characters.deliveredBy: Jonadab the son of Rechab, whose generations-old command the Rechabites still kept; tested and used by Jeremiah as an object lesson to Judah
characters.purpose: The Rechabites' unbroken obedience to a mere human ancestor's command — never drink wine, never build houses, live in tents — shames Judah's refusal to obey the living God, who has spoken to them 'rising early and speaking' through his prophets.
funFacts: Jeremiah sets pots of wine and cups before the Rechabites in a temple chamber and offers them a drink; they refuse, citing Jonadab's ancient command, kept 'unto this day' (35:1-10).
They explain they only came into Jerusalem's walled safety at all because of the Chaldean and Syrian armies invading the land (35:11).
God rewards their fidelity with a promise: 'Jonadab the son of Rechab shall not want a man to stand before me for ever' (35:19).

verses.note: The Rechabites refuse wine, citing their ancestor Jonadab's command.
God's reward of enduring faithfulness in response to their obedience.

characters.name: Ahikam the son of Shaphan
characters.perkNote: Represents protection extended to the prophet — a small loyalty bonus to Jeremiah's tier.

genealogy.note: His son Gedaliah later becomes governor of the remnant after Jerusalem's fall (40:5).

funFacts: Personally intervened to save Jeremiah's life after the temple sermon trial: 'the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, that they should not give him into the hand of the people to put him to death' (26:24).

verses.note: Protects Jeremiah from being handed over for execution.

characters.name: Hanameel
characters.perkNote: Represents the field purchase — a cost-reduction flavor tied to buying land during the siege.

genealogy.father: Shallum, Jeremiah's uncle (32:7) — a different man from King Jehoahaz, who was also called Shallum (22:11); see book notes.
genealogy.note: Jeremiah's cousin, called his 'uncle's son' (32:12).

funFacts: Came to Jeremiah in the court of the prison, exactly as the LORD had forewarned, to offer his field at Anathoth for sale under the right of redemption (32:6-8).
Jeremiah weighed him seventeen shekels of silver for the field and had the deed sealed and witnessed as a legal, permanent record (32:9-12).

verses.note: Sells his field at Anathoth to Jeremiah under the redemption right.

characters.name: Zephaniah the priest
characters.perkNote: Represents the king's repeated, if reluctant, willingness to hear from Jeremiah.

genealogy.note: A priest sent as royal messenger; distinct from the prophet Zephaniah, author of a separate OT book.

funFacts: Sent by Zedekiah to Jeremiah at the start of the siege to ask him to 'inquire... of the LORD for us' (21:1-2).
Sent again later in the siege on a similar errand (37:3).

verses.note: Sent by Zedekiah to ask Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD.
Sent a second time on a similar errand during the siege.

characters.name: The Four Princes (Shephatiah, Gedaliah son of Pashur, Jucal, and Pashur son of Malchiah)
characters.perkNote: A hostile-court flavor, representing the political pressure that lands Jeremiah in the dungeon.

genealogy.note: An undifferentiated group of four royal officials named together at 38:1: Shephatiah the son of Mattan, Gedaliah the son of Pashur, Jucal (Jehucal) the son of Shelemiah, and Pashur the son of Malchiah. This Pashur son of Malchiah is a different man from Pashur the son of Immer (ch. 20) and from Malchiah the son of Hammelech, whose dungeon Jeremiah is cast into (38:6); this Gedaliah son of Pashur is likewise a different man from Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, later governor of Judah — see book notes for both.

funFacts: Told Zedekiah that Jeremiah 'weakeneth the hands of the men of war' and 'seeketh not the welfare of this people, but the hurt,' asking for him to be put to death (38:4).
Zedekiah handed Jeremiah over to them, saying 'he is in your hand: for the king is not he that can do any thing against you' (38:5).

Jucal (as Jehucal) had earlier been sent, alongside Zephaniah, as one of Zedekiah's own messengers to Jeremiah (37:3) — the same man later turns accuser; not a separate naming collision, just one man's changing role.

verses.note: The four princes accuse Jeremiah and have him cast into the dungeon.

characters.name: Malchiah the son of Hammelech
characters.perkNote: A locational flavor only — no independent action beyond owning the dungeon used as a prison.

genealogy.father: Hammelech (possibly a royal title, 'the king's son,' rather than a strict personal name)
genealogy.note: Owner or namesake of the dungeon/cistern in the court of the prison where Jeremiah is cast (38:6); a different man from Pashur the son of Malchiah, one of the four princes who casts him there (38:1) — see book notes.

funFacts: The dungeon Jeremiah is lowered into by cords 'was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire' (38:6).

verses.note: Jeremiah is cast into his dungeon and sinks into the mire.

characters.name: Irijah
characters.perkNote: Represents a false-accusation obstacle — a small negative flavor to production while Jeremiah is imprisoned.

genealogy.note: 'A captain of the ward' at the gate of Benjamin (37:13).

funFacts: Arrested Jeremiah as he tried to leave Jerusalem toward Benjamin during a lull in the siege, accusing him falsely of deserting to the Chaldeans (37:13-14).
Jeremiah denied the charge, but was beaten and imprisoned in a dungeon-house regardless (37:14-16).

verses.note: Arrests Jeremiah on a false charge of desertion.

characters.name: Jehoahaz (Shallum)
characters.perkNote: A brief-reign flavor — minimal ongoing bonus, reflecting his three-month rule.

genealogy.mother: Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah
genealogy.note: Reigned briefly in his father Josiah's place under his throne name Shallum (22:11) before being deposed by Pharaoh Necho in favor of his brother Jehoiakim; a different man from Shallum, Jeremiah's own uncle and Hanameel's father (32:7) — see book notes.

funFacts: Jeremiah prophesies he will never return from exile: 'he shall not return thither any more: but he shall die in the place whither they have led him captive' (22:11-12).

verses.note: Prophecy that Shallum/Jehoahaz will die in exile, never to return.

characters.name: Uriah the son of Shemaiah
characters.perkNote: A martyred-prophet flavor — a cautionary, non-production entry included for narrative completeness.

genealogy.father: Shemaiah of Kirjathjearim — a different Shemaiah from Shemaiah the Nehelamite, the false prophet writing from Babylon against Jeremiah (ch. 29); see book notes.

funFacts: Prophesied 'according to all the words of Jeremiah' against the city and land (26:20).
Fled to Egypt in fear of Jehoiakim, but was fetched back by Elnathan the son of Achbor and others, and executed by the king, his body cast into the graves of the common people (26:21-23).

verses.note: Prophesies like Jeremiah, flees to Egypt, is brought back and executed.

characters.name: Elnathan the son of Achbor
characters.perkNote: A mixed-loyalty flavor — he both fetches a condemned prophet back from Egypt and later pleads against burning Jeremiah's scroll.

genealogy.note: A prince in Jehoiakim's court.

funFacts: Sent to Egypt to bring back the prophet Uriah for execution (26:22-23).

Later one of the princes who, on hearing Baruch's scroll read, urged Jehoiakim not to burn it — 'Elnathan... had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them' (36:25).

verses.note: Pleads unsuccessfully with Jehoiakim not to burn Jeremiah's scroll.

characters.name: Jehudi
characters.perkNote: A minor procedural flavor — facilitates the scroll's destruction, with no independent motive stated in the text.

genealogy.note: Court official sent to fetch and read Baruch's scroll (36:14).

funFacts: Sent by the princes to fetch Baruch and the scroll, then commanded to read it aloud before the king, cutting each read section with a penknife and casting it into the fire as Jehoiakim listened (36:21-23).

verses.note: Reads the scroll aloud to Jehoiakim, who burns it section by section.

characters.name: Seraiah the son of Neriah
characters.perkNote: Represents carrying the family's prophetic work abroad — a loyalty bonus tied to Baruch's tier.

genealogy.note: Baruch's brother (51:59).

funFacts: A 'quiet prince' who went to Babylon with King Zedekiah in the fourth year of his reign (51:59).

Carried a scroll of Jeremiah's judgment oracles against Babylon, was instructed to read it aloud there, then bind a stone to it and sink it in the Euphrates as a sign that Babylon 'shall sink, and shall not rise' (51:60-64).

verses.note: Carries and sinks the scroll of judgment against Babylon in the Euphrates.

characters.name: Nebuzaradan
characters.perkNote: Represents surprisingly favorable treatment of Jeremiah by an enemy official — a loyalty-boost flavor despite being a foreign captain.

genealogy.note: 'Captain of the guard,' Nebuchadrezzar's chief officer over the destruction of Jerusalem (39:9-10).

funFacts: Given charge of burning the king's house and the people's houses and breaking down Jerusalem's walls (39:8).
Personally found Jeremiah bound in chains among the captives, freed him, and gave him the choice to come to Babylon under care or remain in the land (40:1-5).
Appointed Gedaliah governor over those left in the land (40:5).

verses.note: Oversees the burning of Jerusalem and deportation of the people.
Personally frees Jeremiah and gives him a choice of where to go.

characters.name: Azariah the son of Hoshaiah
characters.perkNote: Represents the remnant's defiance of the very answer they swore to obey.

genealogy.note: One of 'the proud men' who stood with Johanan against Jeremiah's word (43:2).

funFacts: Accused Jeremiah of lying about the LORD's command, claiming Baruch had incited him to hand the remnant over to the Chaldeans, and refused to stay in the land (43:2-3).

verses.note: Accuses Jeremiah of lying and refuses his instruction to remain in the land.
